part3: Part Three: Foreign Lands and the Mountain
ch11.title: Fugitives
ch11.b002: Thomas Didymus was the man who managed the itinerary of the apostolic corps. Which road to take, where to sleep, what hour to leave and what hour to arrive: these were his to decide. But the road they took that day was not one he had planned. On Sunday morning, May 22, A.D. 29, there was a sudden commotion at the rear entrance of Zebedee’s house in Bethsaida, and in the noise and the fear of the moment the apostles took the newcomers for the men sent to arrest the Master. They hurried out through the front entrance and down to the waiting boat. There were twenty-five of them: the Master, his twelve apostles, and the twelve evangelists. As they pulled at the oars Thomas tried not to look back. The white walls of Bethsaida grew smaller behind them. He made his reckonings anyway, because he could not help it. They had food for less than three days. Nobody had brought a change of clothes. Worst of all, this was a journey without a day fixed for the return, and Thomas had never in his life set out on a journey like that.
ch11.b003: They came ashore near the village of Kheresa. They left the boat in the keeping of friends and walked a little way to the north, to spend the night in a park south of Bethsaida-Julias. They had camped there before. The trees were familiar, and so was the sound of the spring. And yet the same place was different now. The last time they had come here as guests of the countryside, men with a following and a message. Tonight they had come as men who were being hunted. Thomas spread his cloak under a tree and turned that difference over in his mind. Fugitive. He rolled the word around in his mouth. It tasted bitter, like a green olive.
ch11.b004: Matthew Levi sat on a rock a little apart and looked across the lake. In the dark a few lights of Capernaum flickered on the far shore. One of them was his own house, where his wife and four children were sleeping, and somewhere down that street stood the customs table where he had once sat for so many years. As a publican he had been shunned by his neighbors, but he had never been chased. And the strange thing was that tonight’s flight did not frighten him very much. To be counted among the hunted seemed, if anything, to make him at last a full member of this company. The tax collector was a fugitive now, exactly like the other eleven. Nobody could say he was standing on the safe side of the line.
ch11.b005: Nathaniel could not sleep. It was his duty to look after the families of the twelve, and that morning he had left every one of those families on the other side of the lake. Would the officers from Jerusalem trouble them? If a child fell sick, who would go? There was nothing at all he could do about it tonight, and accepting that required a little philosophy. He lay on his back, looked up through the branches at the stars, and said to himself that if a man could add a cubit to his height by worrying, he would have been a giant by morning.
ch11.b006: Before they lay down for the night the Master called them around him. He told them his plan: to travel through Batanea and northern Galilee and on to the Phoenician coast. Then he asked them to remember how the Psalmist had spoken of such times, in the song about the heathen raging and the kings of the earth taking counsel against the Lord’s anointed. That much, he said, they were now seeing fulfilled before their eyes. But they would not see the rest of the song fulfilled, the part about dashing the nations to pieces with a rod of iron, for the Psalmist had misunderstood the Son of Man and his mission. His kingdom was founded on love, proclaimed in mercy, and established by unselfish service. The Father did not sit in heaven mocking the heathen, and the gentiles would be received with open arms.
ch11.b007: He told them, too, that they who professed to have entered the kingdom were far too vacillating and indefinite. The heathen went straight for their goals; his own followers lingered in a kind of chronic yearning. If their service consisted mostly in regretting the past, whining over the present and hoping vainly for the future, they could hardly call themselves worthy of the kingdom. Let them stop their useless yearning, he said, and go out bravely to do the work of building it.
ch11.b008: Thomas felt the words were aimed at him. Only a few minutes earlier he had been regretting and complaining in exactly that way. Fleeing and going forward, he thought. The same steps on the same road could be counted either way, and the name of the journey would change depending on which way a man counted them. He lay down under his tree and decided that tomorrow he would count today’s steps over again.
ch11.b010: The next morning, Monday, May 23, the company divided. The Master told Peter to take the twelve evangelists over to Chorazin, while he himself, with the other eleven apostles, set out north and east by way of the Jordan and the Damascus road. They reached Caesarea-Philippi on the afternoon of Tuesday, May 24, and there they stayed for two weeks.
ch11.b011: Those two weeks were hard for the eleven. The Master did no public work. The apostles held a number of quiet evening meetings in the city, and believers came out now and then to the camp to talk with him, but very few new believers were won. And Peter was not there. Until he was gone they had not known how much room his voice had taken up among them. He had always been the first awake, talking before anyone else had his sandals on; he asked the questions nobody else asked and said the things nobody else would say. Without him the camp felt oddly large and oddly quiet. One by one the apostles grew less talkative, and before long they were almost depressed.
ch11.b012: Nathaniel was the first to notice it. He looked at Thomas. Thomas was sitting with his arms around his knees, staring for a long time at nothing in particular. Nathaniel knew that face. When Thomas wore it, he avoided people, and above all he avoided the Master. Nathaniel went over and sat down beside him.
ch11.b015: “Then we are in trouble. I have never seen the day when you were not counting something.”
ch11.b016: Thomas did not answer, but the corner of his mouth moved a little. Nathaniel did not try to haul him up out of his mood. He simply stayed where he was, sitting beside him. Not leaving a man alone: that, as far as Nathaniel understood it, was where caring for people began and where it ended.
ch11.b017: Matthew had a different worry. Since the multitudes had begun to fall away from the Master in Galilee, the offerings had dwindled sharply. Every evening Judas Iscariot sat with the money bag on his knees and counted, and every evening the counting was shorter. Matthew watched it out of the corner of his eye. In his head he went over what was left of his own property: how much remained in Capernaum, and through whom he would have to sell it. As always, he said nothing to anyone.
ch11.b018: Even so, in those two weeks they learned a great deal from their daily talks with the Master. They learned that many souls could best be led to love the unseen God by being taught first to love the brothers they could see. And with that, his old saying took on a new meaning for them: that whatever they did for the least of his brethren, they had done for him.
ch11.b019: Around noon on Wednesday, June 8, Peter arrived with the evangelists. They had spent two weeks in Chorazin, preaching to a small but earnest company of believers, and they had won very few new souls. No city in all Galilee yielded so few for the kingdom as Chorazin. Peter’s voice was as loud as ever, but something in it had been bent. That evening, as they told over their experiences among the unbelievers, the Master spoke again of the parable of the sower and taught them at length what the apparent failure of a life’s work really means. Thomas watched Peter’s face and understood that there was a warmth in it, when a man who had failed came home and sat down among his companions, that he had not expected. The camp was noisy again.
ch11.b020: In the Shadow of the Rock near Luz
ch11.b021: On Thursday morning, June 9, after the messengers of David had brought word from Bethsaida about the progress of the kingdom, the twenty-five left Caesarea-Philippi. They went around the marsh country by way of Luz. Thomas walked at the front, choosing the path. He was doing his own work again, and it put a little life back into him.
ch11.b022: Near Luz they stopped for lunch in the shade of an overhanging ledge of rock. Before the bread had even gone around, Peter spoke. If the Father in heaven knew all things, he asked, and if his spirit was their strength in building the kingdom, then why were they running from the threats of their enemies? Why did they refuse to stand up to the foes of truth? Peter had been carrying that question since Chorazin.
ch11.b023: Before the Master could answer, Thomas broke in. He hardly knew he was going to speak until he heard himself. He said he truly wanted to know what was wrong with the religion of their enemies in Jerusalem. What was the real difference between that religion and their own? Why were they so divided in belief when they all claimed to serve the same God? Only when he had finished did Thomas realize that he had cut across Peter’s question. Peter glanced at him.
ch11.b024: The Master said that he did not mean to brush Peter’s question aside. He knew how easily his reasons for avoiding an open clash with the rulers at this time could be misunderstood. But it would help all of them more if he answered Thomas, and he would do so when they had finished eating. Thomas chewed his bread with his face burning. His question had been chosen. He was glad of it, and he was sorry for Peter.
ch11.b025: When the crumbs had been brushed away, the Master began. The religions of the world, he said, had a double origin, natural and revealed. And at any one time, among any one people, three kinds of religion could be found side by side. There was primitive religion, the fear of mysterious forces and the worship of what was stronger than man. There was the religion of the mind, the religion of civilization, which leaned on the authority of established tradition. And there was the religion of the spirit, the religion of revelation, which proved itself in human experience. The religious leaders in Jerusalem, he told them, had taken the teachings of their old teachers and prophets and hardened them into a fixed system of belief, a religion of authority, whose appeal was chiefly to the mind. And now he and they were about to enter a deadly conflict with that religion.
ch11.b026: A religion of authority, the Master went on, was the easy way out. It offered a ready refuge where the distracted soul could hide when fear harassed it and uncertainty tormented it. The price it asked was only a passive, intellectual assent. But the man who chose that path gave up the most thrilling adventure a human being can know: the personal search for truth, the struggle with doubt until faith wins the victory, the adventure of a man seeking God for himself and finding him.
ch11.b027: Thomas held his breath. Doubt wrestled with until faith wins. He set those words on the palm of his hand and weighed them. All his life he had been ashamed of the doubter in himself. Ever since he lost his twin sister when he was nine years old, he had become a man who doubted everything first, and that was why he had never got along easily with people. Yet now the Master was saying that doubt was not something to be thrown out of the religion of the spirit; it was something to be wrestled with. The religion of the spirit, he said, meant effort, struggle and conflict. It meant faith, determination, love, loyalty and progress. Nowhere in that list was there anything about a peace without doubts.
ch11.b028: Then the Master rose. He pointed to each of the twenty-four in turn and called each by name. Thomas heard his own name. Which of them, the Master asked, would rather take the easy road of the fossilized religion the Pharisees defended in Jerusalem? Or would they choose the hardships and persecutions that came with proclaiming a better way to men? Were they fearful, soft and ease-seeking? Were they afraid to trust their future to the God of truth, whose sons they were? Would they go back to the easy certainty of tradition, or would they go forward with him into an uncertain and troubled future?
ch11.b029: The Master rarely appealed to their feelings like this. Almost at once all twenty-four rose to their feet. Peter’s mouth was already open. But the Master raised his hand and stopped them. Do not answer now, he told them. Go apart, each man by himself, and be alone with the Father. Find there an answer that is free of emotion. And when you have found that true answer, speak it freely and boldly to the Father.
ch11.b031: They scattered. Thomas left the shade of the rock and climbed the slope above it. His body was trembling. His heart was stirred, and that unsettled him, because he was a man who did not trust decisions made while his feelings were high. So when the Master told them not to answer yet, Thomas felt as though he were known.
ch11.b032: He sat down on a small rock and looked north. The white summit of Mount Hermon floated above the haze. The easy road or the hard one. He went back over the past year. The excitement of the day five thousand were fed; the synagogue at Capernaum afterward, where people walked out one by one; the flight from Galilee. Judged by arithmetic alone, this road was already going downhill. The crowds had scattered, the money bag was light, and they were men on the run. As a stone it would be a cracked stone. Thomas had been a mason, and a mason does not put a cracked stone into a foundation.
ch11.b033: But he counted other things too. More than two years beside this man. A man who did not lose his temper, who did not hurry, who rebuked his followers but never once drove one of them away. Above all, he had never once driven away Thomas the doubter. Even today he had chosen Thomas’s question, as though he were inviting him to bring his doubts along. Thomas suddenly understood. He was still here, not because he had no doubts, but because even with his doubts he could not leave this man. That was his answer. He spoke it silently toward the sky. I still do not understand all of it. But I will take the hard way.
ch11.b034: When he had finished, the trembling in his body stopped, and he sat there a long while without moving. The wind brushed over the dry grass. Below him the others were sitting alone too, behind rocks and under trees. Matthew was crouched by a ditch; Nathaniel lay on his back looking at the sky. James and John Zebedee sat well apart from each other. Philip wandered about, unable to choose a place. Simon Zelotes stood clenching and unclenching his fists. The Alpheus twins sat under the same tree, back to back. They had been told to go apart, and they had done it in their own way. Thomas saw it and smiled a little.
ch11.b035: After a while Andrew called them together again. Every face was flushed, and some eyes were wet. But the Master did not ask for their answers. He only said that they should resume their journey; they were going into Phoenicia to stay for a season. And he asked them to pray the Father to change these emotions of mind and body into higher loyalties of mind and deeper experiences of the spirit.
ch11.b036: For a while the twenty-four walked in silence. Then one and another began to talk, and soon they were stopping each other in the road to talk, until their pace slowed to almost nothing. By three o’clock in the afternoon they could go no farther, and they came to a halt. Peter went up to the Master. He told him that he had spoken to them the words of life and truth, that they wanted to hear more, and he begged him to go on. Thomas looked at Peter’s back. The man whose question he had taken at lunch was now asking on behalf of them all. Peter was not a man to hold a grudge over such a thing.
ch11.b037: In the shade of the hillside, the Master taught them again about the religion of the spirit. God had not stopped speaking when the old prophets fell silent, he said, and they should not be content to keep quoting those prophets; they should aspire to become living prophets themselves. And they should not try to prove to other men that they had found God, because no such proof could be manufactured. There were, however, two sure demonstrations: the fruits of the spirit showing in their everyday lives, and the fact that they had risked everything they were and everything they had on the adventure of eternal survival.
ch11.b038: Thomas wrote those words deep in his heart. Do not try to prove it. For a man who knew nothing but proofs, it was a strange kind of release. The Father, the Master added, would always respond to the faintest flicker of faith. He honored even the feeble attempts of honest but fearful souls. But they had been called out of darkness into light, and so they were expected to believe with their whole hearts.
ch11.b039: When he had finished, the Master beckoned to Andrew. Then he pointed west, toward Phoenicia, and said:
ch11.b041: Something in Thomas’s chest gave a small, sharp throb. Let’s go: that was what he himself always said, the first one on his feet once a matter was decided. Today, for the first time, he heard his own words come from the Master’s mouth. He shouldered his pack and took the lead. It was not a flight anymore.
ch11.b043: On the afternoon of Friday, June 10, they reached the outskirts of Sidon. On the way into the city they crossed a bridge, the first that many of them had ever seen. As they walked over it the Master remarked that this world was only a bridge: they might pass over it, but they should not think of building a house on it. Nathaniel turned around at once to look at the bridge again. However well a bridge was built, nobody lived on it. He liked the figure very much.
ch11.b044: The Master lodged at the home of a well-to-do woman named Karuska, who had once been a patient in the hospital at Bethsaida in the days when the crowds still followed him. The apostles and evangelists were divided among the houses of her friends close by. That June Sabbath was one of great quiet. They spent it turning over what they had heard about religion on the road to Sidon. Each of them understood something of it; none of them understood all of it.
ch11.b045: That afternoon something happened. The Master had asked them to tell no one he was staying in that house; he wanted to rest. The apostles kept his word. But one of Karuska’s servants went next door to a Syrian woman named Norana and told her that Jesus was there. Norana had a daughter about twelve years old who suffered from a grievous nervous disorder with convulsions, and the mother believed that the child was possessed by an unclean spirit. She appeared at the door holding the girl by the hand.
ch11.b046: The Alpheus twins went out first; managing crowds was their task. Through an interpreter they explained politely that the Master was resting and could not be disturbed. Norana answered that in that case she and her daughter would wait right there until he had finished his rest. Then Peter tried. He told her that the Master was worn out with much teaching and healing and had come to Phoenicia for quiet. It was no use. The woman said she would not leave until she had seen him.
ch11.b047: Then it was Thomas’s turn. He thought he could handle this. Reasoning with people was something he was sure of. Calmly, point by point, he explained why it was not possible to see the Master now. Norana heard him out to the end. Then she said that she had faith the Master could cast out the demon that tormented her child; she had heard of what he had done in Galilee, and she believed in him. And looking Thomas straight in the eye, she asked what had happened to them, his disciples, that they would turn away people who came seeking his help.
ch11.b048: Thomas withdrew. He had nothing to say. Only two days before, on the hillside near Luz, he had told the Father that he would take the hard way, that he would carry a better way to men. And today he was standing in a doorway sending a mother home. His reasoning had no flaw in it. The Master had said he wanted rest; they had only been keeping his word. Yet one sentence from this woman had brought all his reasoning down. He leaned against the wall. His face was hot.
ch11.b049: Last of all Simon Zelotes stepped forward. He looked down at the woman and told her that she was a Greek-speaking gentile, and that it was not right for her to expect the Master to take the bread meant for the children of the favored household and throw it to the dogs.
ch11.b050: Matthew went rigid when he heard it. Dogs. He knew that word. In the years at the customs table he had never forgotten what men like Simon called him: a dog of Rome. He looked at Simon’s back. He and this man ate the same bread now and walked the same roads. Simon no longer called him that. And yet here was the same word falling from the same mouth onto someone else.
ch11.b051: But Norana did not look wounded. If anything, she seemed to be smiling a little. She said that she understood him. In the eyes of the Jews she was only a dog. But as far as his Master was concerned, she was a believing dog. And then she added that surely even he, good man that he was, would not dare to take from the dogs their right to the crumbs that happened to fall from the children’s table.
ch11.b052: Matthew very nearly laughed out loud. He felt he knew this woman. He knew how a despised person learns to catch the contempt thrown at her and turn it aside: not answering with rage, not groveling either, but turning the word over and handing it back. As a former publican he knew how much old pain that kind of wit grows out of. Simon Zelotes had no reply. The back of his neck went red.
ch11.b053: At that very moment the child was seized with a violent convulsion in front of them all. The mother cried out that they could see for themselves that her daughter was possessed. If their need did not move these men, she said, it would move their Master, who she had heard loved all men and even healed gentiles when they believed. They were not worthy to be his disciples. She would not leave until her child was cured.
ch11.b054: Through an open window the Master had heard every word. Now, to their great surprise, he came outside. The apostles stepped aside. He told the woman that her faith was great, so great that he could not withhold what she desired. Let her go in peace, he said; her daughter had already been made whole. And the girl was well from that hour. He asked the mother and daughter to tell no one. But the two of them never stopped telling it, all through the countryside and even in Sidon, so that within a few days he found it wise to change his lodgings.
ch11.b055: That night Simon Zelotes sat alone in a corner of the courtyard. Matthew hesitated over whether to go to him. He did not want to say, Now do you understand? So he drew a cup of water, set it down beside Simon without a word, and turned away. Behind him Simon spoke in a low voice.
ch11.b056: “That woman. She had a way with words.”
ch11.b058: That was all Matthew said. Neither of them said anything more. But that night Matthew heard, in Simon’s voice, that one of its edges had gone a little dull.
ch11.b059: The next day the Master taught the apostles about what had happened. They could see for themselves, he said, how gentiles were able to show saving faith in the gospel of the kingdom. If the children of Abraham were not minded to show faith enough to enter, the Father’s kingdom would be taken by the gentiles. Nor did the Master hide the fact that it was the woman’s humor, as well as her great and persistent faith, that had touched his heart. Once he said to Thomas that his own people took themselves too seriously and had almost no sense of humor. The burdensome religion of the Pharisees, he said, could never have arisen among a people who knew how to laugh; they strained at gnats and swallowed camels. Thomas passed this on to Nathaniel just as he had heard it. Nathaniel laughed for a long time and then said that he must have been suited to this kingdom from the very beginning.
ch11.b061: After that the Master stayed just north of Sidon, at the home of Justa and her mother, Bernice. Every morning he taught the twenty-four there, and in the afternoons and evenings they went into Sidon to teach and preach. The apostles were astonished. The same message that the synagogues of Galilee had bolted their doors against, the people of this gentile city heard with gladness. In a short time many entered the kingdom.
ch11.b062: Nathaniel watched these gentiles for a long time. He was proud of his own people. When he first walked into the streets of Sidon he had drawn his cloak closer around himself without even thinking, because he had grown up being taught that this was unclean ground. But these Greek-speaking people were not afraid of the Master’s words. That God was no respecter of persons or nations, that the universe was governed by unchanging law and could therefore be trusted: these things they accepted more readily than the Galileans had. Some of them came to understand not only that Jesus was like God but that God was like Jesus. Nathaniel thought: it is not that men cannot understand this man. It is that they are afraid to. And the place where that fear was strongest was his own homeland.
ch11.b063: On Tuesday, June 28, they went up the coast to Porphyreon and Heldua and worked there for a week, while the Master went off for three or four days to the city of Beirut. On Wednesday, July 6, they returned to Sidon, and from there they went south along the coast by way of Sarepta, reaching Tyre on Monday, July 11.
ch11.b064: They stayed two weeks in Tyre. Each apostle took one of the evangelists with him, and two by two they taught throughout the city and its surroundings. The Master made his headquarters at the home of a believing Jew named Joseph, who lived three or four miles south of Tyre. Every morning the apostles crossed into the city by way of Alexander’s mole. Matthew loved the fishy reek of shellfish from the dye works and the clamor of the waterfront, where a dozen languages tangled together. Among the leading makers of Tyrian purple, many believed in the kingdom, and Matthew was glad to count some of them among the people he met in those streets.
ch11.b065: On the afternoon of July 20 the Master spoke publicly in Tyre, the only time he did so there. He taught the believers about the Father’s love for all mankind and about the Son’s mission to reveal the Father to every race of men. The interest among the gentiles was so great that the doors of the temple of Melkarth were opened to him. That set Thomas thinking for a long time. The love of the Father was being proclaimed inside the house of a gentile god. A year earlier he would not have believed it possible.
ch11.b066: In that same address the Master told for the first time the story of the white lily. The lily, he said, lifts its clean, snow-white head high into the sunshine while its roots are sunk in the dark muck of the soil below. So it is with men. Even though their roots lie in the animal soil of human nature, they can by faith lift their spirits into the sunlight of heavenly truth and bear the noble fruits of the spirit.
ch11.b067: And in that same sermon he used a parable from his own trade, the first and only one he ever drew from carpentry. Build the foundations of character well, he told them. Do not be like the foolish carpenter who spends his precious time squaring, measuring and smoothing a worm-eaten, rotting beam, only to find, when all the work is done, that it must be thrown out as unfit for the foundation.
ch11.b068: While he listened to that parable Thomas looked down at his own hands. A carpenter’s hands, a mason’s hands. He knew beams like that: sound on the outside, rotten within. Tap one with a hammer and it gave back a different note. How many times in his younger days had he wrestled with timber like that? And now this man, who had held the same tools, was talking about the same timber. For the first time Thomas felt that the Master had hands like his own. Not a great teacher only, but a man who had driven a splinter into his palm at the plane. Strangely, the thought comforted him.
ch11.b070: That evening Nathaniel asked the Master a question he had been carrying for a long time. From the Master’s own teaching, he said, they knew very well that God never leads anyone into temptation. Why then did they pray that God would not lead them into temptation?
ch11.b071: The Master said it was not strange that such a question should arise, since they were beginning to know the Father as he knew him, and not as the early Hebrew prophets had dimly seen him. Their forefathers had seen the hand of God in almost everything that happened and had credited God with both good and evil. But men, he said, are most often led into temptation by their own selfishness and the urges of their animal nature. When temptation came, they should recognize it honestly for what it was and turn the energies that were seeking expression toward higher channels and finer goals. And he warned them against trying to overcome one desire by setting another against it through the mere force of the will. When a man came truly to love the higher thing, the lower would be forgotten in that love. A new and sincere affection, he said, had a mighty power to drive out the old.
ch11.b072: The apostles and evangelists went on asking questions far into the night, and the Master answered many of them. At one of those answers Matthew set down the cup he had been holding. The Master told them not to be discouraged at discovering that they were human. They should not be downcast because they could not wholly forget certain things they regretted. The mistakes they failed to forget in time, he said, would be forgotten in eternity. And they should never judge a soul by a single unfortunate episode.
ch11.b073: Matthew covered his face with his hands. Mistakes he could not forget. He had many of those. The days at the customs table when he set the duty on a poor fisherman’s nets; the day he turned away a widow who wept and clung to his sleeve; his own hard face, unmoved even when his countrymen spat at him. Since becoming an apostle he had never been able to forget those faces. That was why he walked at the very back of the company. That was why he gave his own money under other people’s names. He had always thought of it as a fitting punishment. Not being able to forget was the price he paid.
ch11.b074: And now the Master was telling them not to sit downcast under the weight of such memories. What they could not forget in time would be forgotten in eternity. To Matthew it sounded like words prepared for him alone. It was something larger than forgiveness. Forgiveness he had already received, on the night of the banquet in Capernaum, when the Master sat down at his table. But even after that he had never forgiven himself. Now someone was telling him that one day he might let go even of the memory. Matthew felt tears seeping between his fingers. He made no sound. Nathaniel, sitting beside him, pretended to see nothing and leaned over to trim the wick of the lamp.
ch11.b075: The Master also told them to seek no recognition they had not earned. Love they should receive freely, whether they deserved it or not; but in matters of honor and praise they should honestly seek only what was their own. Matthew raised his head. His secret wish that the Master would somehow know what he had quietly done: on which side of that line did it fall? He could not settle it that night. He only saw the Master’s eyes rest on him for a moment and then move on. They were eyes that knew something. But what exactly they knew, Matthew never did discover.
ch11.b077: The day before they left Tyre, the Master called everyone together and told the twelve evangelists to go back by a different road from the one he and the apostles would take. The evangelists parted from him there. After that they were never again so intimately associated with him.
ch11.b078: About noon on Sunday, July 24, the Master and the twelve left Joseph’s house and went down the coast to Ptolemais. They stayed a day there, comforting the believers, and on the evening of the twenty-fifth Peter preached. The voice that had been bent at Chorazin stood straight again.
ch11.b079: They turned inland, by way of Jotapata and Ramah to the village of Zebulun, and on to Gennesaret on the western shore of the lake, where they had arranged to meet David Zebedee.
ch11.b080: On the road Judas Iscariot said little. In Phoenicia he had carried out his duties without a fault. But Matthew noticed that every so often he would grip the money bag and stare off into the distance. Matthew did not know how Judas felt about their flight from Galilee. Only once he heard Judas mutter, as if to himself, that he had never heard of a deliverer who spent his time hiding along a gentile coast. Matthew made no reply. Andrew must have heard it too, because he slowed his step and walked beside Judas for some while without a word.
ch11.b081: In a short conference with David they learned that many leaders were gathered on the other side of the lake, near Kheresa, and that same evening they crossed over by boat. It was the very water they had fled across ten weeks before. Thomas sat on the gunwale and looked down into it. Back then he had tried not to look behind him. This time he looked ahead. On the same water, he had become a different man.
ch11.b082: They spent a day resting in the hills, and the next day they went to the park where the five thousand had once been fed. They rested there three days and met each day with the believers. About fifty men and women came, all that remained of the once numerous believers of Capernaum and the country around it. Fifty people sat on the grass where five thousand had eaten. But Nathaniel looked at the fifty faces one by one. These were the people who had come through the great sifting and were still here. He thought those faces weighed more than the five thousand.
ch11.b083: Meanwhile the world had shifted a little. The Master’s enemies had decided that the movement was broken, that his haste to withdraw meant he was so frightened he would never come back to trouble them, and active opposition had all but died away. Philip, the brother of Herod, had become a halfhearted believer and sent word that the Master was free to live and work in his territory. Even Herod Antipas sent word that, although he had signed warrants for his arrest in Galilee, he had not authorized any arrest in Perea.
ch11.b084: It was about the first of August, A.D. 29. The scattered, tested and depleted company was gathering again. That night Thomas lay on the grass and traced the road they had come, backward. Kheresa, Caesarea-Philippi, Luz, Sidon, Porphyreon, Tyre, Ptolemais, Jotapata, Ramah, Zebulun, Gennesaret. Not one stretch of it had been his planning. Yet he remembered every step of it. It had begun as a fugitive’s road. Coming back, he found it was a road with another name. He did not yet know that name. But over the whole length of it hung a single sentence he had heard on the hillside near Luz. Let us be on our way.
ch11.b086: The events follow Paper 155, “Fleeing Through Northern Galilee,” and Paper 156, “The Sojourn at Tyre and Sidon”: the landing near Kheresa and the night in the park south of Bethsaida-Julias, with the teaching on the Psalm (155:0.1–1.6); Peter and the evangelists at Chorazin, the eleven at Caesarea-Philippi, and their depression without Peter (155:2.1–3.8); the questions of Peter and Thomas near Luz, the discourse on religion, the appeal to each of the twenty-four by name, the dispersal to pray alone, Peter’s request at three o’clock, the teaching on the religion of the spirit, and “Let us be on our way” (155:4.1–6.19); the bridge, Karuska’s house and the healing of Norana’s daughter, with the twins, Peter, Thomas and Simon Zelotes in that order, and the remark on humor made to Thomas (156:0.1–2.8); Porphyreon, Heldua, Beirut, Tyre, the Melkarth temple, the white lily and the carpenter parable, Nathaniel’s question about temptation and that night’s teaching (156:3.1–5.22); the parting from the evangelists, the return from Ptolemais to the park near Kheresa, and the changed attitude of the enemies, Philip and Herod Antipas (156:5.23–6.10). The departure scene draws on 154:6.11–7.3.
ch11.b087: Character facts come from Paper 139: Thomas as manager of the itinerary, his past as carpenter and mason, his avoidance of Jesus when depressed, his “Let’s go!” and the loss of his twin sister (139:8.2–8.11); Matthew’s family, his secret giving and his shame as a publican, and the early coolness of Simon Zelotes toward him (139:7.1, 7.3, 7.8–7.9); Nathaniel’s pride, humor and care for the apostles’ families (139:6.3–6.7); Judas’s humiliation at the flight from the Pharisees (157:7.2).
ch11.b088: Fictional additions are small: the inner thoughts and memories of Thomas, Matthew and Nathaniel; the descriptions of the lake, the dye works and the hillside; the short exchange between Nathaniel and Thomas; Matthew bringing water to Simon Zelotes and their few words; the content of Thomas’s answer on the hillside; Judas’s muttered remark and Andrew walking beside him; and where each man sat when they went apart to pray.
ch11.b089: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
